forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton Cabinet asked to raise capitalisation directives budget from £2m to £4.561m
news_drafts.lead:
Wolverhampton Council's Cabinet is asked on 18 November to raise its capitalisation directives budget from £2m to £4.561m, an increase of £2.561m. The report says approval for the increase is sought in that report.

The council's forecast papers, in an appendix setting out detailed changes, give the reason as "additional use of capital receipts flexibility to fund specific transformational projects". Capital receipts are the money a council raises from selling assets.

The appendix does not name the projects in the material reviewed. The £2m is the currently approved budget and £4.561m is the proposed figure.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton's high needs schools spending ended 2025-26 £10.4m over, against £6.8m forecast in budget
news_drafts.lead:
Spending on support for children with special educational needs in Wolverhampton ended 2025-26 at £10.4m over budget, the Schools' Forum heard on 15 October. The council's budget in February 2025 had expected an overspend of £6.8m on the "high needs" part of school funding, which covers children with special educational needs and disabilities. Spending was £62.08m against a budget of £51.72m, a 19.9% overrun.

The largest single driver was top-up payments to schools for pupils with special needs. These were £29.62m against a budget of £26.91m, an overspend of £2.72m, or 10%. The paper says the increase was part of the overspend already indicated at the third quarter. Within top-up funding, special schools and alternative provision (education outside mainstream schools) took £1.9m of additional spend, and exceptional needs funding, for specialist equipment and one-to-one support, rose £340,000, or 15%, on the previous year. Independent provision for under-16s within the city ran £0.83m (17%) over, at £5.70m against £4.87m. Provision outside the city came in £0.61m (7%) under.

Other parts of the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) partly offset the overspend. The Schools Block had a £0.5m surplus and the Early Years Block a £0.4m underspend. The net deficit held in the council's unusable reserve for the grant stood at £9.2m at year-end, up £4.3m from £4.9m a year earlier.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton Pensions Board: auditors expect unmodified opinion on £23,368.6m pension fund accounts
news_drafts.lead:
Auditors of the West Midlands Pension Fund expect to give an unmodified opinion, meaning a sign-off without qualification, on its accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026. The draft accounts, in the audit findings report put to the Pensions Board on 13 October 2026, show net assets of £23,368.6m at that date. The report says the audit identified no adjustments affecting the fund's reported financial position and met no significant difficulties or significant matters.

The auditors did identify £20.7m of unadjusted differences in the valuation of the fund's investments as at 31 March 2026, above the £10.9m reporting threshold. The report attributes the overstatement to the timing of information for pension fund reporting compared with the audit date of the underlying investment funds. Management proposes not to amend the statements, on the basis that the differences "are not material both quantitatively and qualitatively".

Testing of employer contributions also found £14.1m of early retirement costs relating to 2024/25 that were recorded in 2025/26. The fund's accounting policy says such contributions are accounted for in the period in which the liability arises. Management assessed the amount as immaterial and made no prior-year restatement. The auditors recommended that management ensure transactions are recognised in line with the fund's accounting policies.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review
findings.headline: Bilston Market re-opened on July 2nd, 2026, after £2.5m of council funds supported £6.6m of external funding for the redevelopment.
findings.detail: The paper says the council investment enabled a full regeneration rather than a reduced refurbishment, including public realm, accessibility and an events space. The paper says the events space was first used on 11 July 2026.
findings.matters: A scheme delivered with a stated ratio of council to external funding is an example that finance directors at other councils may want to compare.
findings.quote: Bilston Market re-opened on July 2nd, 2026, with a purpose-built canopy

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review
findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grant budget rises by £4.3m, assuming the 2027-2028 allocation matches 2026-2027 because it is unconfirmed.
findings.detail: The increase is fully funded by the annual DFG grant allocation from MHCLG. The paper says an update will follow at the next capital monitoring review once allocations are confirmed.
findings.matters: Budgeting on an unconfirmed grant allocation is a risk that finance directors and auditors would check when the allocation is confirmed.
findings.quote: As allocations for 2027-2028 have not been confirmed at the time of writing this report, this is an assumption

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review
findings.headline: Transformational projects capitalisation rises by £2.6m to fund up-front costs of projects that the paper says will deliver ongoing revenue savings.
findings.detail: The paper says the increase uses additional capital receipts flexibility for identified transformational projects. Such projects would access capital funding, if required, for the up-front costs of delivering revenue savings.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts flexibility to fund transformation costs that aim at revenue savings is an approach that finance directors and auditors would scrutinise.
findings.quote: A £2.6 million increase relating to the Transformational Projects capitalisation

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review
findings.headline: Capital receipts assumed in the General Fund total £33.9m, £545k above the approved budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the receipts forecast reflects re-profiled receipts and capital requirements. It also says that only disposals likely to complete are included, and that the forecast will be monitored through the year.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a funding source that depends on asset sales, and a finance director would compare how much of the programme relies on them.
findings.figures: £33.9m capital receipts assumed over 2026-2027 to 2030-2031; £545k increase against the approved budget
findings.quote: This is an increase in a region of £545,000 when compared to the approved budget

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review
findings.headline: External grants and contributions finance 62.3% of the General Fund capital programme.
findings.detail: The paper says the share of external funding is high, most significantly from central government grants and West Midlands Combined Authority funding. It also says the profile of the programme reflects single-year funding settlements and bid-reliant funding.
findings.matters: A high external-funding share ties the programme to grant decisions that are outside the council's control, which is a risk peers and lenders would weigh.
findings.figures: 62.3% of General Fund budget financing from external resources
